care: The Aeneid is a war poem. There are battles and deaths, especially in Books 2, 10, 11 and 12, and Book 4 ends with Queen Dido taking her own life after Aeneas leaves her. The lesson summarizes these parts without detail. For young readers, Books 1, 3, 5 and 8 (the storm, the voyage, the games and the visit to the site of Rome) are the gentlest places to start.

young.html: Long ago the city of Troy was tricked by the Greeks and their wooden horse. One Trojan prince, Aeneas, escaped from the burning city. He carried his old father on his back and held his little son by the hand.

The gods told Aeneas to sail west and find a new home in Italy. The journey took seven years. He met storms, monsters and a queen who wanted him to stay. His people grew tired, and so did he. But he kept going, because he knew others were counting on him. The Romans told this story about themselves: Aeneas’s people became the Romans.

A Roman poet named Virgil wrote the story down as a long poem in twelve parts, called “books.” He called Aeneas pius, which means more than our word “pious.” It means faithful to your family, your country and your gods.

young.cap: Follow Aeneas from Troy to Italy. Tap Next stop, or tap a number on the map.

young.html: Make a shield of the future. In Book 8 the god Vulcan makes Aeneas a shield covered with pictures of Rome’s history, from its founding to the poet’s own day. Draw a round shield on paper and fill it with four or five scenes from your family’s story, from the oldest you know to today. Then tell someone the story, scene by scene.

There are battles in this story. If you read it with a grown-up, the voyage (Book 3), the boat race and games (Book 5) and the visit to the hills where Rome would one day stand (Book 8) are good places to begin.

full.html: Publius Vergilius Maro, called Virgil in English, was born in 70 BC near Mantua in northern Italy and died in 19 BC. He grew up during Rome’s civil wars. When Octavian, Julius Caesar’s heir, defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC and became the emperor Augustus, Virgil had already written the Eclogues and the Georgics. He spent his last ten years on the Aeneid.

The poem gives Rome a founding story as grand as the Greeks’ Homer. Its first six books are a voyage, like the Odyssey; its last six are a war, like the Iliad. It also ties the hero to Augustus, whose family, the Julii, claimed descent from Aeneas’s son Iulus. Virgil died before he had finished revising it. An ancient life of Virgil says he asked for the poem to be burned, and that Augustus would not allow it. Dozens of lines are still unfinished, broken off halfway.

full.text:
Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by fate,
And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate,
Expell’d and exil’d, left the Trojan shore.
Long labors, both by sea and land, he bore,
And in the doubtful war, before he won
The Latian realm, and built the destin’d town;
His banish’d gods restor’d to rites divine,
And settled sure succession in his line,
From whence the race of Alban fathers come,
And the long glories of majestic Rome.
full.author: Virgil
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son
full.note: Dryden’s translation was first published in 1697.

full.html: The Latin begins Arma virumque cano, “Arms and the man I sing.” In two words Virgil names his two models: arma, war, for the Iliad, and virum, the man, for the Odyssey.

head: Books
What happens
rows: Juno, who hates the Trojans, sends a storm. Aeneas lands near Carthage, a new city ruled by Queen Dido.
At Dido’s feast Aeneas tells of Troy’s fall and of his seven years of wandering.
Dido and Aeneas fall in love. Mercury, sent by Jupiter, reminds Aeneas of his duty. He leaves, and Dido dies in despair.
Funeral games in Sicily for his father, Anchises.
With the Sibyl of Cumae, Aeneas visits the underworld. Anchises shows him the great Romans of the future.
In Latium, King Latinus offers peace, but Juno stirs up war with the Rutulian prince Turnus. Aeneas finds allies at Pallanteum, where Rome will one day stand.
War in Italy. Evander’s son Pallas is killed by Turnus. In the last scene Aeneas defeats Turnus in single combat.

full.text: Pietas: the hero who carries others

full.html: Virgil’s word for Aeneas is pius. His pietas is loyalty to the gods, to his father and son, and to his people’s future. The poem’s most famous picture of it comes on the night Troy falls.

full.text:
‘Haste, my dear father, (’t is no time to wait,)
And load my shoulders with a willing freight.
Whate’er befalls, your life shall be my care;
One death, or one deliv’rance, we will share.
My hand shall lead our little son; and you,
My faithful consort, shall our steps pursue.’
full.author: Virgil
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: Duty costs him. He loses his wife Creusa in the flight from Troy. He leaves Dido, whom he loves. Leading tired people, he hides his own fear, as in his speech to the crew after the storm in Book 1.

full.text:
“Endure, and conquer! Jove will soon dispose
To future good our past and present woes.
…
An hour will come, with pleasure to relate
Your sorrows past, as benefits of Fate.”
full.author: Virgil
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: Virgil’s Latin for the last idea is famous: forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit, “perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things.” Readers have quoted it in hard times for two thousand years.
In the underworld, Anchises shows Aeneas a parade of future Romans and tells him what Rome’s gift to the world will be.

full.text:
But, Rome, ’t is thine alone, with awful sway,
To rule mankind, and make the world obey,
Disposing peace and war by thy own majestic way;
To tame the proud, the fetter’d slave to free:
These are imperial arts, and worthy thee.
full.author: Virgil
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: Readers disagree about how to take passages like this. Some read the Aeneid as a celebration of Rome and of Augustus. Others point to how much grief the poem gives to the losers: Dido, Turnus, and young men on both sides who die in the war. Many find both voices in it, and think Virgil meant them to be heard together.

Thinking Virgil invented Aeneas. Aeneas is already a Trojan hero in Homer’s Iliad, where a god predicts that he and his descendants will survive Troy. Roman writers had linked him with Rome’s founding long before Virgil. Virgil’s achievement was the poem, not the legend.

items: Schools: the Aeneid was the main Latin schoolbook for centuries, in Roman times and long after. Augustine, later on this ladder, learned it as a boy.
Dante: in the Divine Comedy, Virgil himself is Dante’s guide through Hell and up the mountain of Purgatory.
Words: phrases like “I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts” (Laocoön’s warning about the wooden horse, Book 2) and “the tears of things” (lacrimae rerum, Book 1) came into many languages.

deep.text: Context: an epic for a new age

deep.html: Virgil wrote after a century of civil wars, when Augustus was building a new order while claiming to restore the old Republic. The poem reaches back to the past to explain the present: Book 6 names Augustus, and the shield in Book 8 shows his victory at Actium in 31 BC. Virgil also received the patronage of Augustus’s friend Maecenas. Whether this makes the poem propaganda, or a poet’s honest hopes and doubts about his age, is one of the oldest debates about it.

The poem ends abruptly. Turnus, beaten, asks for mercy, and Aeneas almost spares him. Then he sees the belt Turnus took from young Pallas, whom Aeneas had promised to protect, and in anger he kills him. The poem stops there, with no wedding, no founding and no peace. Some readers see justice, others a hero failing his father’s advice “to spare the conquered.” Virgil leaves the reader to decide.

items: When duty and love pull in opposite directions, how should a person choose? Was Aeneas right to leave Dido?
Can a story that celebrates a country also be honest about what its rise cost other people?
Is it fair to judge an ancient hero by our standards, or only by his own?

deep.html: Augustine, in the Confessions, regrets that as a boy he wept for Dido and not for his own soul. In the City of God he quotes Virgil often, and argues against the hope that any earthly city, Rome included, will last forever. Dante made Virgil his guide. Milton’s Paradise Lost, much later on this ladder, opens as an epic in the same grand tradition, and the poet Tennyson called Virgil “lord of language.”

questions: Aeneas carries his father and leads his son. What do you owe to the people older and younger than you in your family?
Was Aeneas right to leave Dido to go on with his mission? What would you have done?
“Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things.” Is there a hard time you are glad, now, to remember?
Virgil asked for the poem to be burned because it was unfinished. Why do you think Augustus saved it? Was he right?
Which matters more in a leader: being brave, or being faithful to the people who depend on him?
The poem makes the reader feel for Rome’s enemies too. Why might a poet do that in a poem about his own country?
